This chapter squeezes chapters 00 to 25 into one review sheet. It teaches nothing new. Every row is a fact, rule or trap that a chapter already established, with a link back to that chapter.

Domains appear in exam-weight order, so the first pages are worth the most items. Facts the chapters couldn't confirm against the documentation are kept apart. They sit in labelled Verify before exam boxes and are collected again in section 16.
5b025cbc6d: Final week: read one domain block per day, in weight order. If you can't explain a row in a sentence, open the linked chapter's summary table and work through its scenarios.
0d3d0cce6b: Format of rules: the "If X then Y" rules are phrased the way exam stems are written. A constraint word in the stem (X) selects a mechanism (Y).
cfd97bf20c: Shared facts for the 5.x models: a 1M-token context window and 128K max output (older models have a 200K window). The cache read multiplier is 0.05 on Opus/Sonnet 5.5 and 0.1 on Haiku 5.5. Sources: Ch 15, 13.
7da7776a8d: Selection order: prompt first, effort second, tier third. Decide per step, by eval, not per application by reputation.
e4a4ed7191: Cheapest that passes: in the ch15 worked example, Sonnet 5.5 at low effort passed at 93% for a third of the Opus cost. Haiku failed the bar. The exam point is the method (eval each candidate, then price the ones that pass), not the numbers.
f0ddecae89: Mixed tiers: orchestrator/worker and executor/advisor designs put most tokens on cheap models. In capstone 2, Haiku lookups were 76% of input tokens but only 15% of cost.
2ac889f32f: Routing/cascade: cost = c_small + p_esc x c_large. Escalate on validator failure, never on self-reported confidence. Every router needs its own eval.
ed0aad2c25: Breaking changes on upgrade to 5.5: non-default sampling params, prefill, budget_tokens and forced tool_choice all become 400s. Two things change silently: the tokenizer (+~30% since Opus 4.7) and the thinking/effort defaults. So recount tokens, replay evals, canary, and keep the pinned rollback.
1450253f0f: Lifecycle: Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired. Retired IDs fail. Start migrating at the deprecation notice, not on the retirement date.
de8d35196b: SDK defaults: 2 retries (3 attempts) on connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx. The SDK honours retry-after and allows a 10-minute timeout per attempt. It may refuse a long non-streaming request and tell you to stream. Ch 05, 14
9c36900817: The prefix hash runs over tools → system → messages and needs an exact match. You get at most 4 cache_control breakpoints. Writes happen only at breakpoints; reads look back ~20 blocks.
dac197bf9b: Minimum cacheable size: 512 tokens on 5.x, 4,096 on Haiku 4.5. Below it nothing is cached, and nothing errors either.
1069d6b9ae: Invalidation: tool edits invalidate everything. A system edit or fast-mode toggle invalidates system + messages. Changes to tool_choice, images or thinking/effort invalidate messages. The self-inflicted ones are timestamps, unstable ordering and edited history.
693bfe0464: Checkpointing: move the breakpoint to the last block each turn (automatic caching does this for you). Keep effort/thinking/tool_choice constant. Warm the cache before a parallel fan-out.
e45fb6983d: Measure token hit rate, write ratio and net saving. A hit rate of zero after a deploy means you should diff the prefix. Ch 15
979a3475ef: You pay 50% of standard price, and only for succeeded requests. Same model, same quality. Processing is async within 24 h, most within 1 h, with no latency SLA.
9bbbf718dc: Limits: 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch. Results come back as JSONL in any order (join on custom_id) and stay available for 29 days. Batches are workspace-scoped.
39ad455ff9: Lifecycle: in_progress → (canceling) → ended. Ended does not mean success. Result types are succeeded (still check stop_reason), errored (invalid: fix it; server: resend), expired (resend) and canceled.
1e2be5def4: One request is one assistant turn, so there's no client tool loop. Pre-fetch the data, run tool rounds between batches, or use realtime.
6485061cd8: Resubmit only the failed custom_ids, tracked in a ledger. Cap the attempts and dead-letter the rest. Poll with backoff (30 s, doubling to ~10 min), and set a cut-off with a realtime fallback.
199238b381: Caching in batch is best-effort (30-98% hits). Use identical prefixes and the 1-h TTL, and group requests by prefix. Ch 07, 24c
b3bfe8869f: The schema subset has no recursion, no external $ref, no numeric/length bounds and no open objects. Unsupported constraints move to your validator.
4b5458c388: Bash prefix rules need the space (Bash(npm run test *)). The legacy :* works only at the end. Compound commands are split, and every part must be covered.
554a20b50f: Paths: ./ is project, / is the settings source, // is absolute, ~/ is home. Only Read and Edit rules govern files. A Read deny covers cat and redirects but not arbitrary programs. Bash rules are not a sandbox.
693fca966a: Project files can't set auto or bypassPermissions. Project allow rules wait until the workspace is trusted.
fec3078a9e:
Contract: the hook gets JSON on stdin (tool_name, tool_input, cwd, transcript_path, ...). What happens next depends on the exit code:

  • Exit 0: stdout is parsed as JSON. It can carry hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision (allow/deny/ask/defer), permissionDecisionReason, updatedInput and additionalContext, plus the universal continue, stopReason and systemMessage.
  • Exit 2: the call is blocked and stderr goes to Claude. This beats allow rules.
  • Any other exit: non-blocking, so the action proceeds. A crashing guard therefore fails open, unless it catches everything and exits 2.

Hooks run in parallel, and deny > defer > ask > allow. A hook allow does not skip deny/ask rules. Ch 20
7ea0d8859a:
The CI mapping used in chapter 11 and capstone 4:

  • killed (124/143) = infra, exit 3;
  • no result line, MCP init errors, is_error/non-success subtype, or non-empty permission_denials = run failed, exit 2;
  • blocking findings in structured_output = exit 1;
  • otherwise 0.

5a8eb20d42: 2026-07-28 (newer): drops the initialize handshake. It's stateless: _meta carries protocolVersion and clientCapabilities on every request. It adds server/discover and -32022 for an unsupported version. There are no sessions, and input_required results replace server-initiated requests.
e77e589cb8: The exam guide (v1.0, July 2026) predates the new spec. Expect questions written against 2025-11-25. An option that describes the handshake isn't wrong for that reason alone. Ch 22, 24b
21a5e38fba: Decision order: guarantee, capability, knowledge, invocation, isolation, then distribution. The common correct layering is MCP for access, Skill for how to use it, subagent for isolation, hook for the must-never, plugin to ship. Ch 23
8dafb562e3: Untrusted content (web, RAG, files, tool results, MCP metadata, memory) enters as data, escaped, in a tool_result or tagged user content. It never goes in the system prompt.
82020a5782: Lethal trifecta check: are private data, untrusted input and egress all in one context? Then remove an edge or gate the egress.
a3ed064394: The principal comes from the session, never from the model. Every tool runs ownership checks. Retrieval gets an ACL pre-filter. Every cache/store key includes the tenant.
291f26adfc: Hooks for the must-never: PreToolUse deny (exit 2 or JSON deny). Guards fail closed, and org policy lives in managed scope. A sandbox/proxy is the floor.
532462ea57: Secrets never go in prompts, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, repos or client apps. Use ${VAR} and secret stores, a backend proxy, and short-lived tokens via WIF. When you rotate, wait ≥ cache TTL. If a secret leaks, revoke it first.
cb3918b4bb: Test with injection cases, N trials each, and impact-based scoring. Gate in CI, and monitor verdicts and canaries in production.
9adbbbf070: These are the items the chapters marked "check the docs". The reasoning around each one is stable. The names and numbers may not be. If an exam option hinges on one of them, prefer the option whose reasoning is right.
904e844a47:
Tie-breaks:

  • Fix the root cause named in the stem.
  • For "first" or "least effort", pick the cheapest change that addresses the cause (often a description or criteria).
  • For irreversible, financial or legal consequences, pick the deterministic control.
  • Prefer the answer that preserves information (structured errors, provenance, custom_id).
